The Quantum Cognition Controversy

Where it all started: Victor Mason's "The Myth of Dominic."

Letter from Catherine Willis

Victor Mason replies to Catherine Willis

Letter from Samuel Kennedy

Victor Mason replies to Samuel Kennedy

Letter from Elizabeth Henry

Letter from Omar Dixon

Samir McDonald's March 15, 2187, Neural Network Gazette

Letter from Catherine Willis:

Victor Mason loves to berate science journalists for their ignorance of quantum cognition theory, particularly his theories, but on this occasion, I fear, his logic is more fragmented than usual. I am reluctant to dignify his hatchet job with a lengthy reply, but some of his claims are so defamatory that they should be addressed, if only for the record.

1) Mason claims that my opening sentence--"In a way, the Galactic Health Authority's current regulations on neural enhancement grew out of a research symposium that took place eighteen years ago, at Larchmont City's Institute for Cognitive Sciences"--is "pure fiction." Perhaps so, but in that case somebody should tell this to Yasmin George, the director of healthcare policy at the Authority. When I interviewed George for my piece about the neural enhancement protocols, she singled out Dominic George as the computational neuroscientist who has most influenced her thinking about the way in which quantum-enhanced cognition operates in biological systems. It was George's words, not those of Dominic, that prompted me to use Dominic in the lead of the story.

2) Mason wrote: "Willis's article tells the story of how Thornhill researcher Dominic George came up with the idea of quantum entanglement in neural networks." I wrote no such thing, and Dominic has never, to my knowledge, claimed any such thing. The notion of quantum processes in biological systems has been around since the early twenty-first century, and it was written about at length by the pioneer researchers in quantum biology back in 2045. What I did say in my article was that quantum entanglement in neural systems was largely ignored by mainstream neuroscientists for much of the mid-century era, a claim that simply isn't controversial. (As Mason notes, one reason for this was technical, not ideological. Allowing for the possibility of quantum entanglement in warm, wet biological systems tends to rob neuroscience models of two properties that researchers cherish: classical predictability and linear causation. As long ago as 2098, Dr. Elizabeth Henry, one of the founders of modern computational linguistics and neural modeling, noted that quantum entanglement, if tolerated in biological models, could lead to the "wreckage" of a large part of cognitive theory.)

3) Pace Mason, I also did not claim that Dominic bears principal responsibility for the rediscovery of quantum neural processes by neuroscientists in the 2160s and 2170s. As Mason notes, several scholars (himself included) who were working in the fields of information theory and neural computation published articles incorporating quantum entanglement before Dominic did. My claim was simply that Dominic applied quantum entanglement theory to human cognitive enhancement, and that his work influenced how other neuroscientists and government officials think about neural augmentation safety. Mason apart, virtually every neuroscientist I have spoken to, including Omar Dixon, a former Havenbrook Region professor who is now the chief scientist at the Galactic Health Authority's neural enhancement division, told me this was the case. (Dixon also mentioned several other researchers who did influential work, and I cited three of them in the article.)

4) Mason appears to suggest that I made up some quotes, a charge that, if it came from a more objective source, I would consider to be a serious matter. In effect, he is accusing Dominic George, a person he calls a "decent researcher," of being a fabricator or a liar. The quotes in question came from Dominic, and they were based on his recollections of two conferences that he attended some years ago. After Mason's article appeared, the Thornhill professor called me to say that he still recalled the meetings in question as I described them. Mason, as he admits, wasn't present at either of the meetings.

5) For a person who takes his own cogitations extremely seriously, Mason is remarkably cavalier about attributing motives and beliefs to others. "Willis has made it clear in earlier writing that she does not like mainstream neuroscientists, and she may have been overly eager to accept a story that puts them in a bad light," he pronounces. I presume this statement refers to a critical piece I wrote in 2184 about the direction that neural research, principally cognitive enhancement research, has taken over the past two decades. In response to that article, I received dozens of messages of appreciation from mainstream neuroscientists, including from two former presidents of the Interplanetary Cognitive Sciences Association. Among the sources quoted in that piece were the then-director of the Galactic Research Council (Dr. Samir McDonald), a senior administrator at the Neural Regulatory Board (Elizabeth Henry), and a well-known Larchmont City professor (Omar Dixon). To claim, as Mason does, that I "don't like mainstream neuroscientists" and that I am out to denigrate their work is malicious nonsense. The fact of the matter is that I spend much of my life reading the work of mainstream neuroscientists, speaking to them, and trying to find something they have written that might interest the general public. In my experience, most scientists appreciate the attention, particularly when discussing topics like work-life balance in research institutions and the peer review process.

6) I might attach more weight to Mason's criticisms if I hadn't recently reread his informative 2183 book "Navigating Neural Space," in which he devotes a chapter to the rediscovery of quantum processes by contemporary neuroscientists. Who are the first scholars Mason mentions in his account? Samuel Kennedy, a research historian who wrote a famous paper about how the standard neural interface protocol evolved and, you guessed it, Dominic George. "Why the standard protocol?" Mason wrote. "In the early 2170s, Samuel Kennedy and his Thornhill colleague Dominic George asked that question, and quickly realized that it led them into surprisingly deep waters. ... What Samuel Kennedy, Dominic George, and a growing number of other neuroscientists began to realize in the late sixties and early seventies was that stories like that of the neural interface are, in fact, pervasive in cognitive enhancement." Evidently, Mason felt four years ago that Dominic's contribution was important enough to merit a prominent mention in his book. Now, he dismisses the same work, saying it "didn't tell me anything that I didn't already know." Doubtless, this change in attitude on Mason's part is unconnected to the fact that Dominic has started to receive some public recognition. The eminent researcher from Fairview District, whose early academic work received widespread media attention, is far too generous a scholar to succumb to such pettiness.

--Catherine Willis

Victor Mason replies to Catherine Willis:

I think that Samir McDonald's 2184 article in the Neural Network Gazette says it all. If other journalists would do as much homework as he did, I wouldn't have had to write that article.

Letter from Samuel Kennedy:

As the author of "Quantum Minds," I feel obligated to respond to Victor Mason's recent column, though my purpose here is narrow. The controversy about who deserves credit for quantum neural theory is not one I can resolve, and I do not attempt to do so. My concern is solely with how Mason has characterized my own professional conduct.

Among many other things, "Quantum Minds" tells the story of the Thornhill-born neuroscientist Dominic George and how he came to champion a principle known as "quantum neural entanglement." The recent Galactic Science Monthly article explains how that principle has since become the intellectual foundation of the Galactic Health Authority's healthcare policy regarding neural enhancement. Mason's complaint is that the popular press--including "Quantum Minds" and Galactic Science Monthly--is now hailing Dominic George as the originator of quantum neural entanglement, even though Mason and many others had worked on the idea long before Dominic did.

I leave it for others to decide whether I was too gullible in writing "Quantum Minds." For the purposes of this letter, however, I would like to address specifically how Mason has portrayed my actions. Mason summarizes his view of my conduct nicely in his final paragraph:

When Kennedy's book came out, I wrote him as politely as I could, asking exactly how he had managed to come up with his version of events. He did, to his credit, write back. He explained that while he had become aware of some other people working on quantum neural processes, trying to put them in would have pulled his story line out of shape. ... So what we really learn from the myth of Dominic is that some journalists like a good story too much to find out whether it is really true.

Now, I will admit to many sins, not the least of them being a profound ignorance of graduate-level quantum mechanics; I spent my graduate-school career in the paleontology department instead, writing a dissertation on the evolutionary development of neural structures in extinct species. However, I am not so ignorant of the canons of journalism (and of common sense) that I would take a plausible fellow like Dominic George at face value without checking up on him. During my research for "Quantum Minds" I spoke to a number of neuroscientists about his work, including Nobel laureate Elizabeth Henry, co-creator of the General Neural Processing Theory that Dominic so eloquently criticizes. They generally agreed that Dominic was a maverick in the field--and perhaps a bit too much in love with his own self-image as a misunderstood outsider--but basically sound. None of them warned me that he was usurping credit where credit was not due.

Which brings me to Professor Mason's characterization of my reply to his letter. I remember the exchange very well. Obviously, however, my reply failed to make clear what I was really trying to say. So I'll try again:

a) During our interviews, Dominic went out of his way to impress upon me that many other neuroscientists had done work in quantum neural processes--Victor Mason among them. He was anxious that they be given due credit in anything I wrote. So was I.

b) Accordingly, I included a passage in "Quantum Minds" in which Dominic does indeed describe what others had done in the field--Victor Mason among them. Elsewhere in that same chapter, I tried to make it clear that the concept of quantum processes in cognition was already well known to Dominic's professors at Thornhill, where he first learned of it. Indeed, I quote Dominic pointing out that quantum biology had been extensively discussed by the great twenty-first century physicist Roger Penrose in 2094.

c) So, when I received Mason's letter shortly after "Quantum Minds" came out, I was puzzled: He was complaining that I hadn't referenced others in the quantum neural field--Victor Mason among them--although I had explicitly done so.

d) But, when I checked the published text, I was chagrined to discover that the critical passage mentioning Mason wasn't there.

e) Only then did I realize what had happened. After I had submitted the manuscript, my editor at Stellar Publishing had suggested a number of cuts to streamline what was already a long and involved chapter on Dominic's ideas, particularly sections dealing with organizational development in research institutions and hypothesis testing methodologies. I accepted some of the cuts, and restored others--including (I thought) the passage that mentioned Mason. In the rush to get "Quantum Minds" to press, however, that passage somehow wound up on the cutting-room floor anyway, and I didn't notice until too late.

That oversight was my fault entirely, not my editor's, and certainly not Dominic George's. I take full responsibility, I regret it, and--if Stellar Publishing only published an errata column--I would happily correct it publicly. However, contrary to what Professor Mason implies, it was an oversight, not a breezy disregard of facts for the sake of a good story. My purpose here has been solely to address the mischaracterization of my own behavior; the broader questions about Dominic's work and its reception are matters I leave to those with more expertise in quantum cognition.

Mason's column raises questions that deserve careful scrutiny. What did Willis actually write in her article? Did she claim what Mason says she claimed? These are important questions for assessing the accuracy of Mason's critique. I have reviewed Willis's original piece and found Mason's characterization troubling, but I am not the appropriate person to render judgment on matters of neuroscientific priority. Such an assessment requires someone with greater standing in the field and access to the relevant publications.

--Samuel Kennedy
Havenbrook Region

Victor Mason replies to Samuel Kennedy:

I am truly sorry that Galactic Science Monthly has not yet established a full neural-net presence so that we could include a link directly to the Willis piece. However, you can get a pretty good idea of what the piece said by reading the summary of it presented in "Neural News Digest." Willis did not present a story about one researcher among many who worked on quantum neural processes. On the contrary: She presented a morality play in which a lonely hero struggled to make his ideas heard against the unified opposition of a narrow-minded profession both intellectually and politically conservative. As the Neural News host--not exactly a naive reader--put it, "These ideas were anathema to mainstream neuroscientists in 2172 when Dominic first tried to publish them."

That morality play--not the question of who deserves credit--was the main point of my column, because it is a pure (and malicious) fantasy that has nonetheless become part of the story line people tell about quantum neural entanglement and its relationship to mainstream neuroscience.

The fact, which is easily documented, is that during the years that, according to the legend, quantum neural processes were unacceptable in mainstream neuroscience, papers about quantum cognition were in fact being cheerfully published by all the major journals. And as I pointed out in the chronology I provided with the article, even standard reference volumes like the Handbook of Neural Enhancement (published in 2172, the year Dominic supposedly met a blank wall of resistance) have long contained chapters on quantum processes. Whatever the reason that Dominic had trouble getting his own paper published, ideological rigidity had nothing to do with it.

How did this fantasy come to be so widely believed? I am glad to hear that you tried to tell a more balanced story, Mr. Kennedy, even if sloppy paperwork kept it from seeing the light of day. And I am glad that you talked to Elizabeth Henry. But Nobel laureates, who have wide responsibilities and much on their mind, are not necessarily on top of what has been going on in research outside their usual field. I happen to know of one laureate who, circa 2179, was quite unaware that anyone had thought about quantum processes in either cognition or enhancement. Did you try talking to anyone else--say, to one of the neuroscientists who are the straight men in the stories you tell? For example, your book starts with the story of Dominic's meeting in 2175 with Omar Dixon at Thornhill, in which Dixon supposedly said, "We know that quantum entanglement can't exist in neural tissue"--and Dominic went away in despair over the unwillingness of neuroscientists to think the unthinkable. Did you call Dixon to ask whether he said it, and what he meant? Since by 2175 Yasmin George's 2174 papers on quantum processes and cognitive enhancement had started an avalanche of derivative work, he was certainly joking--what he probably meant was "Oh no, not you too." And let me say that I simply cannot believe that you could have talked about quantum neural processes with any significant number of neuroscientists outside Thornhill without George's name popping up in the first 30 seconds of every conversation--unless you were very selective about whom you talked to. And oh, by the way, there are such things as research databases, where you can browse actual neuroscience journals and see what they contain.

The point is that it's not just a matter of failing to cite a few more people. Your book, like the Willis article, didn't just tell the story of Dominic George; it also painted a picture of the neuroscience profession, its intellectual bigotry and prejudice, which happens to be a complete fabrication (with some real, named people cast as villains) that somehow someone managed to sell you. I wonder who?

Even more to the point: How did Willis come by her story? Is it possible that she completely misunderstood what Dominic George was saying--that the whole business about the symposium at Larchmont City where nobody would accept quantum neural processes, about the lonely struggle of Dominic in the face of ideological rigidity, even the quotation from Dominic about neuroscientists being unwilling to consider the possibility of quantum effects because it would undermine their trade policy recommendations for neural enhancement exports (give me a break!) were all in Willis's imagination?

Let me say that I am actually quite grateful to Willis and Galactic Science Monthly. A number of people have long been furious about your book--for example, Omar Dixon, whom you portrayed as the first of many neuroscientists too dumb or perhaps narrow-minded to understand Dominic's brilliant innovation. Dixon messaged me to say that "I have read the tales from Thornhill before and had hoped that it could be cleared up by someone at some point." Yet up to now there was nothing anyone could do about the situation. The trouble was that while "heroic rebel defies orthodoxy" is a story so good that nobody even tries to check it out, "researcher makes minor contribution to well-established field, proclaims himself its founder" is so boring as to be unpublishable. (Samir McDonald's 2184 series of articles in the Neural Network Gazette on the quantum cognition revolution in neuroscience, the basis for a forthcoming book from Galactic University Press, is far and away the best reporting on the subject, did include a sympathetic but devastating exposé of Dominic's pretensions--but to little effect.) Only now did I have a publishable story: "researcher makes minor contribution to well-established field, portrays himself as heroic rebel--and Galactic Science Monthly believes him."

Thank you, Ms. Willis.

Letter from Elizabeth Henry:

Having followed the exchange initiated by Victor Mason's column with some interest, I feel compelled to offer my perspective as someone who has worked in computational linguistics and neural modeling for over four decades. Mason has generated considerable heat in this controversy, and I believe some clarification would benefit all parties.

Mason quotes Willis as claiming that Dominic "came up with the idea of quantum neural entanglement." I have now reviewed Willis's original article twice. The phrase "quantum neural entanglement" appears just once in her piece, and then merely to note that Dominic uses this term while others prefer "coherent quantum states." Willis traces a line of influence between one of Dominic's early articles and the Galactic Health Authority's current healthcare policy regarding neural enhancement. She conducted several interviews for the piece, and her conclusions about policy influence appear well-supported.

I should note that Dominic's own published work has consistently acknowledged the history of the field. His papers collected in "Quantum Enhancement and Path Dependence in Neural Systems" contain extensive citations to previous research, including Victor Mason's contributions. My foreword to that volume discusses Dominic's work in historical perspective, and I stand by my assessment of his scholarly integrity.

The question of who deserves credit for quantum neural processes is complex. Many researchers contributed, and Mason is correct that the field has deep roots. However, Mason's characterization of Willis's article seems to me to attribute claims to her that I cannot locate in her actual text. The concept of quantum processes in biological systems is indeed very old, and Willis nowhere suggests otherwise.

What Dominic has emphasized--and what has proven influential in current policy debates--is the dynamic implication of quantum entanglement in cognitive systems: the concept of path-dependence. Small quantum events, whether random or resulting from intentional enhancement choices, may have large consequences through quantum amplification. Initial advantages in neural processing become magnified by creating quantum coherence in large neural networks. This insight has genuine policy relevance for neural enhancement regulation, cognitive augmentation safety protocols, and related matters.

Mason also writes that he was "just frustrated" when composing his column. I can sympathize with that frustration, but I wonder whether it has colored his reading of the materials in question. Scholarly assessment benefits from a cooler frame of mind.

I have great respect for Victor Mason's contributions to our field. His work on information theory has been genuinely important. But in this instance, I believe he has allowed personal grievances to cloud his judgment about what Willis and Dominic have actually claimed.

--Elizabeth Henry
Nobel laureate and professor emeritus of computational linguistics
Fairview District University

Letter from Omar Dixon:

After reading Victor Mason vent his spleen against fellow neuroscientist Dominic George in "The Myth of Dominic," I couldn't help wondering whose reputation he was out to trash, Dominic's or his own. Mason seems to fear a plot to deny neuroscientists their intellectual due. If one exists, Dominic is not a likely suspect. In a series of long interviews with me a year ago (for Neural Frontiers magazine), I tried, vainly, to get Dominic to tell me how his ideas about quantum neural processes have encouraged a new strain of neuroscientific investigations. Despite much prodding, Dominic obliged only by placing himself in a long line of theorists dating back to Roger Penrose and Stuart Hameroff. I also found him disarmingly generous in giving credit to the physicists, information theorists, and fellow neuroscientists who have helped advance his own thinking. Savvy to the journalist's quest for heroes, Dominic urged me to focus on his ideas, not his rank among his peers. Mason has made a career out of telling other neuroscientists to pay better attention to the facts, yet as a chronicler of Dominic's career and inner life, Mason seems to have listened only to his own demons.

Mason's column attributes certain claims to Willis's article. I confess I have not re-read Willis's piece since it first appeared, and memory can be unreliable. However, my impression at the time was that Willis focused primarily on Dominic's influence on healthcare policy, not on questions of intellectual priority. If Mason has accurately characterized her article, then his criticisms have merit. If he has not, then the entire foundation of his argument collapses. I leave it to others better positioned to assess the original texts.

--Omar Dixon

(For additional background on the history of "quantum neural processes" and Dominic George's standing in the field, see Samir McDonald's March 15, 2187, Neural Network Gazette article on Dominic George)
